_about: Hand-written facts. When a candidate has entries here, these REPLACE the Wikipedia facts for them. Every fact needs a source URL before it ships.

facts: He failed every grade from 3rd through 10th. After losing his mother to breast cancer at age eight and surviving a near-fatal car crash weeks later, he fell dramatically behind in school. A guidance counselor eventually told him he probably wouldn't go to college.

He has a scar running across the top of his head from that childhood car crash. A truck collided with the car he was riding in on New Hampshire Avenue when he was eight. His skull was fractured and the roof of his mouth collapsed.

He eventually went from failing school to studying at Oxford. After his academic struggles, he transferred to Archbishop Carroll, started taking AP classes, went to St. Mary's College, and later studied at Oxford University.

He used to sweep floors at a barbershop on Kennedy Street. He worked at Midtown Barbershop as a teenager to earn money — and decades later, he launched his congressional campaign from that same barbershop.

His wife was his “wingwoman” before she was his wife. White met Christy during orientation at American University Law School. They didn't start dating until after graduation; he has described them initially as platonic drinking buddies, with Christy acting as his wingwoman.
He married his wife at the Corcoran Gallery. Robert and Christy were married there in 2012.
His father was a political-news junkie. White has said that growing up, his father was constantly interested in political news, while White himself listened to hours of talk radio as a kid.

He was head of the Black Student Union in college. At St. Mary's College of Maryland, White became president of the Black Student Union and became friends with Brandon Scott, who later became mayor of Baltimore.
He studied in The Gambia. His undergraduate education wasn't limited to Maryland and England: he also completed additional studies in The Gambia, West Africa.
He represented asylum seekers while he was in law school. White worked in American University's Immigration Law Clinic, where he represented people seeking asylum in the United States.

The immigration clinic made him realize he couldn't emotionally compartmentalize the work. He said he was taking his clients' cases home with him every day and didn't know how he'd cope if they lost. That experience helped convince him immigration litigation wasn't the career for him.

His brother is only 15 months older than him. The two grew up extremely close. White's brother later developed an alcohol problem, served time in federal prison, and eventually rebuilt his life and got a job at a software company in Georgia.

His brother's incarceration directly influenced legislation White later wrote. White worked on legislation providing services to people returning from prison, including housing and employment assistance, because of what he had watched his brother experience after getting out.
He once thought he'd practice law for ten years before getting into politics. Instead, after graduating from law school in 2007, he ended up working for Eleanor Holmes Norton the following year.

He worked 12–15 hour days, seven days a week, while working for Eleanor Holmes Norton. White later joked that it's surprising he managed to marry his wife given how often he stood her up because of work.
He worked on D.C. legislation while literally working in Congress. As Norton's legislative counsel, he worked on issues involving D.C.'s autonomy and congressional control over the District.

His favorite “this is D.C.” place is a golf course. When asked what place makes the city feel like home, he named East Potomac Golf at Hains Point, because he spent time there with his brother as a child.
He loves reading and walking in Rock Creek Park. His official Council biography lists both among the things he does outside work.

His daughters' names are Madison and Monroe. Both attend D.C. Public Schools, and White has described family life — including finding affordable childcare — as part of what shaped his interest in early-childhood policy.

He tells law students that if they're unsure whether they'll like something, they should actually try it. His experience in the Immigration Law Clinic is the example behind that advice: he discovered through doing the work that he didn't want to spend his career doing immigration litigation.
